cards.q: How are alcohols classified as primary, secondary or tertiary?
cards.a: By the number of carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries the OH group: one (primary), two (secondary) or three (tertiary).
cards.why: Methanol, with no other carbon, behaves as a primary alcohol.

cards.q: Name this alcohol and classify it as primary, secondary or tertiary.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butan-2-ol: a four-carbon chain with an OH group on the second carbon.

cards.a: Butan-2-ol: a secondary alcohol.
cards.why: The carbon bonded to the OH group is bonded to two other carbons.

cards.q: Name this compound and say whether it is a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropan-2-ol: a central carbon bonded to three methyl groups and an OH group.

cards.a: 2-methylpropan-2-ol: a tertiary alcohol.
cards.why: The carbon bonded to the OH group is bonded to three other carbons.

cards.q: True or false: this alcohol is branched, so it is a secondary alcohol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropan-1-ol: a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon and OH on an end carbon.

cards.a: False. It is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, a primary alcohol.
cards.why: Only the carbon carrying the OH group matters, and here it is bonded to just one other carbon.

cards.q: Write the equation for the fermentation of glucose.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow  2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 2CO_{2}}\)
cards.why: Enzymes in yeast catalyse the reaction.

cards.q: State and justify the conditions used to make ethanol by fermentation of glucose.
cards.a: Yeast, in aqueous solution, at about 35 °C, with air kept out.
marks: Yeast provides the enzymes that catalyse the reaction.
About 35 °C (30 to 40 °C): a compromise between a reasonable rate and denaturing the enzymes at higher temperatures.
Anaerobic (no air): otherwise the yeast respires aerobically and ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid.

cards.q: How is ethanol separated from the mixture produced by fermentation?
cards.a: Fractional distillation.
cards.why: Ethanol boils at a lower temperature than water, so it distils off first. The ethanol can then be used as a biofuel.

cards.q: What is a biofuel?
cards.a: A fuel made from biological material (biomass) that has recently been living, such as ethanol from sugar cane or maize.
cards.why: Biofuels are renewable: the crop can be regrown. Fossil fuels formed from organisms that died millions of years ago.

cards.q: Write equations to support the statement that ethanol made by fermentation is carbon neutral.
cards.a: Six \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) are absorbed by photosynthesis, and six are released by fermentation (2) and combustion (4).
marks: Photosynthesis: \(\mathrm{6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O \rightarrow C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2}}\)
Fermentation: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 2CO_{2}}\)
Combustion: \(\mathrm{2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 6O_{2} \rightarrow 4CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O}\)
Net: 6 \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) absorbed and 6 released, so no overall change.

cards.q: Give reasons why bioethanol is not truly carbon neutral.
cards.a: Energy, often from fossil fuels, is used to plant, fertilise and harvest the crop, make fertilisers, transport the materials and distil the ethanol. This releases extra carbon dioxide.
cards.why: The equations only count the carbon in the crop itself.

cards.q: Discuss the environmental and ethical issues of using land to grow crops for bioethanol.
cards.a: Benefits: renewable, and closer to carbon neutral than petrol. Problems: land and water that could grow food.
marks: Bioethanol is renewable and saves crude oil.
Land used for fuel crops is not used for food, which can raise food prices: an ethical issue where people go hungry.
Forests may be cleared to grow crops, destroying habitats and releasing carbon dioxide.
Fertilisers and pesticides can pollute water.

cards.q: Give the conditions for the industrial hydration of ethene to ethanol.
cards.a: Steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst, at about 300 °C and 60 atm.

answerFigure.alt: Ethene and steam react over a phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 °C and 60 atm to give ethanol.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CH_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH}\). Unreacted ethene is recycled.

cards.q: Outline the first part of the mechanism for the acid-catalysed hydration of ethene: how the carbocation forms and how water attacks it.
cards.a: Electrophilic addition of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), then attack by water.

answerFigure.alt: Hydration mechanism, first part: the C=C bond attacks an H+ ion, giving a carbocation; a lone pair on the oxygen of a water molecule then attacks the positive carbon.

marks: A curly arrow from the C=C bond to the \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion, giving a carbocation.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on the O of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) to the positive carbon.
This gives the protonated alcohol, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH_{2}^{+}}\).

cards.q: Outline the last step of the mechanism for the hydration of ethene, starting from \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH_{2}^{+}}\), and explain why the acid is a catalyst.
cards.a: An O–H bond breaks to release \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), giving ethanol.

answerFigure.alt: Hydration mechanism, last part: in the protonated ethanol, an O–H bond on the positive oxygen breaks, its electrons going to the oxygen, releasing H+ (the catalyst) and giving ethanol.

marks: A curly arrow from an O–H bond to the positive oxygen, releasing \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).
The \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) used in the first step is regenerated, so the acid is a catalyst.

cards.q: Compare making ethanol by fermentation with making it by hydration of ethene.
cards.a: Fermentation: renewable raw material, low temperature, but slow, a batch process, and impure (needs distilling). Hydration: fast, continuous and gives purer ethanol, but uses ethene from crude oil (finite) and needs high temperature and pressure.
cards.why: Which is better depends on whether a country has plenty of crops (such as sugar cane) or of crude oil.

cards.q: Write an equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + 3O_{2} \rightarrow  2CO_{2} + 3H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Ethanol is used as a fuel, often blended with petrol.

cards.q: Write an equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{7}OH + 4\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Or doubled: \(\mathrm{2C_{3}H_{7}OH + 9O_{2} \rightarrow 6CO_{2} + 8H_{2}O}\). Count the oxygen atom in the alcohol when balancing.

cards.q: What reagent is used to oxidise alcohols, and what colour change is seen?
cards.a: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid). It turns from orange to green.
cards.why: Orange \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\) is reduced to green \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\).

cards.q: True or false: the green colour seen when an alcohol is oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI) is the colour of the organic product.
cards.a: False. The green colour is from \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) ions; the organic products are colourless.
cards.why: The dichromate(VI) ions are reduced as the alcohol is oxidised.

cards.q: What do primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols give when heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
cards.a: Primary: an aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid. Secondary: a ketone. Tertiary: no reaction (not easily oxidised).
cards.why: The colour change from orange to green shows that oxidation has happened.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [O], for the oxidation of ethanol to an aldehyde.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + [O] \rightarrow  CH_{3}CHO + H_{2}O}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethanol is oxidised by [O] from acidified potassium dichromate(VI), distilling as it forms, to give ethanal and water.

cards.why: The product is ethanal. [O] stands for oxygen from the oxidising agent.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [O], for the oxidation of ethanal to a carboxylic acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHO + [O] \rightarrow  CH_{3}COOH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethanal is oxidised by [O] from acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux, to give ethanoic acid.

cards.why: The product is ethanoic acid. No water forms in this step.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [O], for the complete oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + 2[O] \rightarrow  CH_{3}COOH + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Two [O] are needed: one to make the aldehyde and one to oxidise it further.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [O], for the oxidation of propan-2-ol, and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3} + [O] \rightarrow CH_{3}COCH_{3} + H_{2}O}\)
Propanone

answerFigure.alt: Propan-2-ol is oxidised by [O] from acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to give propanone and water.

cards.why: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones, which are not oxidised further.

cards.q: Explain how a primary alcohol is oxidised so that the main product is the aldehyde, not the carboxylic acid.
cards.a: Distil the aldehyde off as soon as it forms.
marks: Add the oxidising agent to an excess of the alcohol (so the oxidising agent is not in excess) and heat gently.
Distil the aldehyde off immediately as it forms.
The aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol (no hydrogen bonding between its molecules), so it leaves the flask before it can be oxidised further.

cards.q: Explain how a primary alcohol is oxidised fully to a carboxylic acid.
cards.a: Heat with excess oxidising agent under reflux, then distil off the acid.
marks: Use an excess of acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
Heat under reflux, so the aldehyde formed first cannot escape and is oxidised further.
Then distil to separate the carboxylic acid.

cards.q: What is heating under reflux, and why is it used?
cards.a: Heating a mixture in a flask with a vertical condenser, so vapours condense and drip back into the flask.
cards.why: Volatile reactants and products cannot escape, so the mixture can be heated for a long time and the reaction goes to completion.

cards.q: In a distillation to collect a product, where should the thermometer bulb be, and why are anti-bumping granules added?
cards.a: The bulb should be level with the side arm leading to the condenser, to measure the temperature of the vapour that is distilling. Anti-bumping granules make boiling smooth, preventing large bubbles.
cards.why: Collect the fraction that distils within a degree or two of the product’s boiling point.

cards.q: Name the two oxidation products of this alcohol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butan-1-ol: a four-carbon chain with an OH group on an end carbon.

cards.a: Butanal (the aldehyde) and then butanoic acid (the carboxylic acid).
cards.why: This is butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol: the carbon chain length stays the same.

cards.q: Explain why tertiary alcohols are not easily oxidised.
cards.a: The carbon carrying the OH group has no hydrogen atom.
marks: Oxidation of an alcohol removes a hydrogen atom from the carbon bonded to the OH group (and the H of the OH), forming C=O.
In a tertiary alcohol that carbon has no H, so a C=O cannot form without breaking a C–C bond.

cards.q: True or false: tertiary alcohols are oxidised to ketones by acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
cards.a: False. Tertiary alcohols are not easily oxidised: the dichromate stays orange.
cards.why: Secondary alcohols give ketones; tertiary alcohols do not react.

cards.q: How can acidified potassium dichromate(VI) distinguish a tertiary alcohol from primary and secondary alcohols?
cards.a: Warm each with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Primary and secondary alcohols turn it from orange to green; a tertiary alcohol leaves it orange.
cards.why: To tell primary from secondary, test the product for an aldehyde.

cards.q: Describe how Tollens’ reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone.
cards.a: Warm with Tollens’ reagent in a water bath. An aldehyde gives a silver mirror; a ketone gives no change.
cards.why: The aldehyde is oxidised and \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) is reduced to silver. Ketones are not oxidised.

cards.q: Describe how Fehling’s (or Benedict’s) solution distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone.
cards.a: Warm with the solution. An aldehyde turns it from blue to a brick-red precipitate; a ketone leaves it blue.
cards.why: The aldehyde reduces blue \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) to red copper(I) oxide, \(\mathrm{Cu_{2}O}\).

cards.q: An alcohol is oxidised and the product is distilled off. The distillate turns Fehling’s solution brick red. Was the alcohol primary, secondary or tertiary?
cards.a: Primary.
cards.why: The distillate is an aldehyde, which only a primary alcohol gives.

cards.q: 6.00 g of propan-2-ol (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60.0\)) is oxidised, and 4.06 g of propanone (\(M_{\text{r}} = 58.0\)) is collected. Calculate the percentage yield.
cards.a: 70.0%
steps: Moles of propan-2-ol \(= \frac{6.00}{60.0} = 0.100\) mol, so at most 0.100 mol of propanone.
cards.why: The reaction is 1 : 1, so moles of product expected = moles of alcohol.

cards.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert an alcohol into an alkene.
cards.a: Heat with an acid catalyst: concentrated phosphoric acid (or concentrated sulfuric acid).

answerFigure.alt: Ethanol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid; water is eliminated, giving ethene.

cards.why: Water is eliminated, so this is an elimination (dehydration) reaction.

cards.q: Outline the first part of the mechanism for the acid-catalysed dehydration of propan-2-ol, up to the formation of the carbocation.
cards.a: Protonation of the OH group, then loss of water.

answerFigure.alt: Dehydration mechanism, first part: a lone pair on the oxygen of propan-2-ol attacks an H+ ion; in the protonated alcohol, the C–O bond breaks with its electrons going to the oxygen, so water leaves and a carbocation forms.

marks: A curly arrow from a lone pair on the O to an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion.
The protonated alcohol has \(\mathrm{OH_{2}^{+}}\) on the carbon.
A curly arrow from the C–O bond to the O: water leaves, giving a carbocation.

cards.q: Outline how the carbocation formed from propan-2-ol becomes propene in the dehydration mechanism.
cards.a: It loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from a neighbouring carbon.

answerFigure.alt: Dehydration mechanism, second part: the carbocation loses H+ from a carbon next to the positive carbon; the C–H bond electrons form the C=C bond, giving propene.

marks: A curly arrow from a C–H bond on the carbon next to the positive carbon to between those two carbons.
The C=C bond forms and \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) is released: the catalyst is regenerated.

cards.q: Butan-2-ol is dehydrated. Name the three alkenes that can form.
cards.a: But-1-ene, E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of three alkenes: but-1-ene (double bond at the end of the chain), E-but-2-ene (the two end carbons on opposite sides of the central double bond) and Z-but-2-ene (the two end carbons on the same side).

cards.why: The H can be lost from carbon 1 or carbon 3; the double bond in but-2-ene gives E and Z isomers.

cards.q: Why is making alkenes by dehydrating alcohols useful for the plastics industry?
cards.a: Ethanol from fermentation can be dehydrated to ethene, which can be polymerised, so addition polymers can be made without monomers from crude oil.
cards.why: This uses a renewable raw material instead of a finite one.

cards.q: Outline how a pure sample of cyclohexene is made from cyclohexanol.
cards.a: Heat cyclohexanol with concentrated phosphoric acid and distil off the impure cyclohexene. Shake the distillate with water in a separating funnel and keep the upper (organic) layer. Dry it with an anhydrous salt, such as anhydrous calcium chloride, then distil again, collecting the fraction at the boiling point of cyclohexene.

answerFigure.alt: Cyclohexanol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid; water is eliminated, giving cyclohexene.

cards.why: Washing removes water-soluble impurities such as acid; the drying agent removes remaining water.

cards.q: In the preparation of cyclohexene, how do you know the organic layer is dry after adding anhydrous calcium chloride?
cards.a: The liquid turns from cloudy to clear.
cards.why: Add drying agent until some stays free-flowing rather than clumping, then decant or filter it off.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanol with phosphorus(V) chloride, and say what is seen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + PCl_{5} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}Cl + POCl_{3} + HCl}\)
Steamy (misty) fumes of hydrogen chloride.

answerFigure.alt: Ethanol reacts with phosphorus(V) chloride at room temperature to give chloroethane, phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3) and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: The fumes are a test for an OH group (alcohols and carboxylic acids).

cards.q: How is an alcohol converted into a bromoalkane using potassium bromide?
cards.a: Heat with potassium bromide and 50% concentrated sulfuric acid. These make HBr in the flask, which reacts with the alcohol.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{KBr + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow KHSO_{4} + HBr}\), then \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + HBr \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}Br + H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: How is an alcohol converted into an iodoalkane?
cards.a: Heat under reflux with red phosphorus and iodine, which react to form phosphorus triiodide, \(\mathrm{PI_{3}}\), in the flask.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{3C_{2}H_{5}OH + PI_{3} \rightarrow 3C_{2}H_{5}I + H_{3}PO_{3}}\)

cards.q: True or false: a bromoalkane is made from an alcohol using concentrated sulfuric acid at full strength with potassium bromide.
cards.a: False. The sulfuric acid is diluted to about 50%.
cards.why: Fully concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises some of the HBr to bromine, and can dehydrate the alcohol.

cards.q: Write an equation for the chlorination of 2-methylpropan-2-ol with concentrated hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{3}COH + HCl \rightarrow  (CH_{3})_{3}CCl + H_{2}O}\)

answerFigure.alt: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is shaken with concentrated hydrochloric acid at room temperature to give 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and water.

cards.why: The product is 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Tertiary alcohols react quickly with concentrated HCl at room temperature.

cards.q: In making 2-chloro-2-methylpropane from 2-methylpropan-2-ol and concentrated HCl, why is the crude product washed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, and what precaution is needed?
cards.a: To neutralise and remove leftover acid. Carbon dioxide forms, so the separating funnel must be vented (tap opened, inverted) often to release the pressure.
cards.why: Afterwards wash with water, dry with anhydrous sodium sulfate, and distil.

cards.q: In a separating funnel, how do you know which layer is the organic product?
cards.a: Add a little water: the layer that gets bigger is the aqueous layer. Otherwise use densities: the denser liquid is the lower layer.
cards.why: Halogenoalkanes with heavier halogens are often denser than water, so they can form the lower layer.
